whatTheyArgued: Dai Zhen (1724-1777) argued that philology and close study of classical language, institutions and terms are the necessary route to understanding the Way (comparing neglect of philology to crossing a river without a boat), and that this must ground, not replace, philosophical interpretation; in ethics he rejected the Neo-Confucian suppression of desire and feeling. Read via SEP only; no primary text (no PD translation found, manifest copyrighted_deferred).

scholarship.supports: philology as foundation for grasping the dao; evidential learning necessary but insufficient
scholarship.disputes: Scholars dispute how accurate his reading of Song-Ming thinkers was, whether his ethics is utilitarian or non-consequentialist, and how far evidential learning shaped his philosophy. The entry does not discuss verifying quotations to source.

ourUse: quotes.js: every quotation is verified against the source bytes (verbatim / drifted-and-backported / unlocated and not printed as a quote), no model in the loop.

bends.ours: Compendium: 'no word is taken on another's say-so — a quotation is traced to and verified against its actual source, or it is not printed as a quotation.'
bends.theirs: I could not verify that Dai Zhen stated this rule; the scholarship I read credits him with philological grounding of interpretation, not a quotation-verification rule. It is kaozheng's general ethos at best.

bends.ours: Evidential research reduced to string containment of quotes.
bends.theirs: Dai's philology is about meaning of terms, institutions, glosses, and he held it insufficient alone; ours is a byte match.
His works are old, but the project's manifest records no usable PD translation (copyrighted_deferred); the entry is not backed by a verified snip.

bends.ours: Drifted quotes are rewritten to source bytes (backport).
bends.theirs: Correcting a text against better witnesses is kaozheng practice in spirit, but this repair rule is ours and not his.

fix: compendium work: 'Evidential-research (kaozheng) scholar who grounded interpretation of the classics in philological study. Our quotes.js is in that spirit: a quotation is the source's bytes or is not printed as one. The rule itself is ours.'
